summary: Miglitol is an oral alpha-glucosidase inhibitor used as an adjunct to diet and exercise to improve glycemic control in adults with type 2 diabetes. By reversibly inhibiting intestinal alpha-glucosidases, it delays carbohydrate digestion and primarily lowers postprandial blood glucose. Unlike acarbose, miglitol is well absorbed but is not metabolized; it is eliminated unchanged by the kidneys and does not cause transaminase elevations. Dose-related gastrointestinal effects (flatulence, diarrhea, abdominal discomfort) are most common and tend to lessen with time. Used alone it does not cause hypoglycemia, but when combined with a sulfonylurea or insulin, low blood sugar must be treated with glucose (dextrose), not sucrose, whose breakdown miglitol blocks.

moa: Miglitol, a desoxynojirimycin derivative, produces its antihyperglycemic effect by reversibly inhibiting membrane-bound intestinal alpha-glucoside hydrolase enzymes in the brush border of the small intestine. These enzymes normally hydrolyze oligosaccharides and disaccharides to glucose and other monosaccharides; their inhibition delays glucose absorption and lowers postprandial hyperglycemia. In contrast to sulfonylureas, miglitol does not enhance insulin secretion, so its glycemic effect is additive when combined with a sulfonylurea and it diminishes the insulinotropic and weight-increasing effects of these agents. It has only minor activity against lactase and is not expected to cause lactose intolerance at recommended doses.

absolute: Inflammatory bowel disease, colonic ulceration, or partial intestinal obstruction (or predisposition to obstruction)
Chronic intestinal diseases with marked disorders of digestion or absorption, or conditions that may worsen with increased intestinal gas formation
Hypersensitivity to miglitol or any component
relative: Significant renal impairment (serum creatinine >2 mg/dL or CrCl <25 mL/min - not recommended)
Concurrent sulfonylurea or insulin (hypoglycemia risk; consider lowering their dose)

preg: Pregnancy Category B. The safety of miglitol in pregnant women has not been established, and there are no adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women. Animal reproduction studies in rats and rabbits revealed no evidence of fetal malformations attributable to miglitol; maternal and/or fetal toxicity (reduced fetal weight, delayed ossification) occurred only at the highest doses tested. Because animal data are not always predictive of human response, use miglitol during pregnancy only if clearly needed; insulin is generally preferred for diabetes in pregnancy.
lact: Miglitol is excreted in human milk to a very small degree - total excretion accounted for about 0.02% of a 100 mg maternal dose, with estimated infant exposure of roughly 0.4% of the maternal dose. Although these levels are exceedingly low, it is recommended that miglitol not be administered to a nursing woman.
renal: Because miglitol is excreted primarily unchanged by the kidneys, accumulation is expected in renal impairment, with plasma levels rising in proportion to the degree of dysfunction. Patients with creatinine clearance <25 mL/min taking 25 mg three times daily showed a greater than two-fold increase in plasma levels. Dosage adjustment to correct this is not feasible because miglitol acts locally in the gut, and little safety data exist in this group. Treatment is not recommended in patients with significant renal dysfunction (serum creatinine >2.0 mg/dL).
hepatic: No dosage adjustment is needed for hepatic impairment. Because miglitol is not metabolized, its pharmacokinetics are not altered in cirrhotic patients relative to healthy subjects, and no influence of hepatic function on its kinetics is expected. Unlike acarbose, miglitol is not associated with dose-related transaminase elevations.

major: Sulfonylureas or insulin - additive glucose lowering increases hypoglycemia risk; consider reducing their dose and treat hypoglycemia with glucose (dextrose), not sucrose
moderate: Intestinal adsorbents (e.g., charcoal) and digestive enzyme preparations with carbohydrate-splitting enzymes (e.g., amylase, pancreatin) - may reduce miglitol effect; do not take concomitantly
Ranitidine - bioavailability reduced by about 60% when given with miglitol
Propranolol - bioavailability reduced by about 40% when given with miglitol
minor: Glyburide - trend toward modestly lower Cmax/AUC (not statistically significant)
Metformin - mean AUC/Cmax about 12-13% lower (not statistically significant)
Digoxin - reduced plasma levels in healthy volunteers, but no change in digoxin-treated diabetic patients
interactions.food: Must be taken with the first bite of each main meal; effect depends on dietary carbohydrate. Antacids do not affect miglitol pharmacokinetics.
interactions.alcohol: Limit alcohol; it can disturb glycemic control.
interactions.diagnostics: Low serum iron occurred more often than with placebo but usually did not persist or affect hemoglobin. No report-marketing hepatic enzyme effects expected; warfarin and nifedipine pharmacokinetics/pharmacodynamics are unaffected.

serious: Hypoglycemia when combined with a sulfonylurea or insulin
emergency: Severe hypoglycemia in combination therapy (use IV glucose or glucagon)
Complications of pneumatosis cystoides intestinalis (e.g., intestinal perforation, hemorrhage, obstruction)

monitoring: 1-hour postprandial plasma glucose to guide titration to the minimum effective dose
HbA1c (glycosylated hemoglobin) approximately every 3 months for long-term control
Routine self-monitoring of blood and/or urine glucose
Gastrointestinal tolerance, especially in the first few weeks
Signs of hypoglycemia when used with a sulfonylurea or insulin
counsel: Take each dose with the first bite of your main meals, three times a day
Gas, bloating, soft stools, and diarrhea are common at first and usually lessen with time

Miglitol alone does not cause low blood sugar, but if you also take a sulfonylurea or insulin and have low blood sugar, use glucose (dextrose) tablets or gel - ordinary table sugar will not work because this medicine blocks its breakdown
Keep a fast-acting glucose source on hand if you take a sulfonylurea or insulin, and make sure family members recognize and can treat low blood sugar
Continue your prescribed diet, regular exercise, and routine blood/urine glucose testing
pk: Acts locally in the gut at each meal
Plasma peak in 2-3 hours (25 mg fully absorbed; 100 mg 50-70% absorbed)
Effect spans each meal; dosed three times daily

pearls: Targets postprandial hyperglycemia and does not cause hypoglycemia when used as monotherapy
Treat hypoglycemia (in combination therapy) with glucose/dextrose, NOT sucrose - miglitol blocks sucrose breakdown
Unlike acarbose, miglitol is well absorbed but not metabolized - eliminated unchanged renally and does NOT cause transaminase elevations (no LFT monitoring required)
GI side effects are dose-related and the main tolerability issue - titrate slowly over weeks
Not recommended if serum creatinine >2 mg/dL (or CrCl <25 mL/min); no dose adjustment needed for hepatic impairment
missed: If you miss a dose at the start of a meal, you can still take it during that meal; if the meal is finished, skip the dose and take the next one with your next main meal. Do not double up to make up for a missed dose.
overdose: Unlike sulfonylureas or insulin, a miglitol overdose will not cause hypoglycemia. It may produce transient increases in flatulence, diarrhea, and abdominal discomfort. Because miglitol lacks extra-intestinal effects, no serious systemic reactions are expected; manage supportively.
